To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of stroke unit care is associated with improved survival, functional outcome, and quality of life in patients with acute ischemic stroke.

(a) stroke unit care is more effective than care on general medical wards in improving survival and functional outcome, but not in improving quality of life; and (b) the effect is greatest for patients with severe stroke.
the 18-month survival of stroke patients treated in stroke units is 20% greater than for those treated in general medical wards and that the difference is maintained at least for 3 years.

the development of new, efficient and reliable methods for solving the problem of the optimal control for nonlinear distributed parameter systems.
the effects of a stroke unit on the functional outcome of patients after stroke.
the development of new and more efficient ways of delivering stroke rehabilitation services.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence that the stroke units are better than the traditional care in general medical wards.
the use of a stroke unit is associated with a significant reduction in mortality, morbidity, length of hospital stay and the need for institutionalization.
the results of the RANTTAS II study indicate that stroke unit care, compared with conventional care, is associated with a significant reduction in the 1-year mortality rate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results of this trial do not support the routine use of stroke units.
stroke units reduce the death rate by 25% to 30%.
the stroke unit model is effective for the acute care of stroke patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of stroke unit care in patients with acute stroke is associated with better functional outcome at 3 months and with a lower rate of death and disability at 1 year.
